command.description: The system command to be executed. To execute multiple commands, separate them with '&&'. For example, 'dir && echo done'.

message.content:
I don’t have a way to probe your connection from here, so I can’t tell you the exact download/upload speed right now.  
But you can run a quick test yourself—either with a web‑based speed‑test or with a short PowerShell script that downloads a known file and measures how long it takes. Below are two common approaches:

---

## 1. Use a Web Site (easiest)

1. Open a browser and go to one of the popular speed‑test sites:
   * https://www.speedtest.net/
   * https://fast.com/ (Netflix)
   * https://www.google.com/search?q=speed+test (Google’s built‑in test)
2. Click “Go” or “Start” and wait for the test to finish.  
   The page will show you:
   * **Download speed** (Mbps)
   * **Upload speed** (Mbps)
   * **Ping** (ms)

---

## 2. Run a PowerShell Command (for more control)

If you prefer a command‑line test, you can use PowerShell to download a file from a public server and time the operation. Here’s a ready‑to‑run script that will:

* Download a 100 MB test file from Hetzner (a reliable public server).
* Measure the elapsed time.
* Compute the average download speed in Mbps.

```powershell
# PowerShell script – copy & paste into a PowerShell window

$uri      = "https://speed.hetzner.de/100MB.bin"   # 100 MB test file
$dest     = "$env:TEMP\hetzner_test.bin"          # temporary location
$stopwatch = [System.Diagnostics.Stopwatch]::StartNew()

# Download the file
(New-Object System.Net.WebClient).DownloadFile($uri, $dest)

$stopwatch.Stop()

# File size in bytes
$bytes = (Get-Item $dest).Length
# Elapsed time in seconds
$seconds = $stopwatch.Elapsed.TotalSeconds
# Speed in megabits per second (Mbps)
$mbps = ($bytes * 8) / ($seconds * 1_000_000)

Write-Host "Downloaded $([Math]::Round($bytes / 1MB, 2)) MB in $([Math]::Round($seconds, 2)) s"
Write-Host "Average speed: $([Math]::Round($mbps, 2)) Mbps"

# Clean up
Remove-Item $dest -Force
```

### How to run it

1. Open **PowerShell** (search for “PowerShell” in the Start menu).
2. Paste the script above and press **Enter**.
3. Wait for the download to finish; the script will print the speed.

> **Tip:** If you want to test upload speed, you’ll need a server that accepts uploads (e.g., a cloud storage bucket or a dedicated speed‑test API). The above script only measures download speed.

---

## 3. Using `speedtest-cli` (Python)

If you have Python installed, you can install the official Speedtest CLI and run it from the command line:

```bash
pip install speedtest-cli
speedtest
```

It will automatically pick the best server, test download/upload speeds, and report the results.

---

### Quick Summary

| Method | What it gives you | How to use |
|--------|-------------------|------------|
| Browser speed‑test | Download, upload, ping | Visit a site and click “Go” |
| PowerShell script | Download speed (Mbps) | Copy/paste script into PowerShell |
| `speedtest-cli` | Download, upload, ping | Install via pip, run `speedtest` |

Pick the method that feels most comfortable for you. If you run into any issues or need help interpreting the results, just let me know!
